ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure there is a square, and the centers of four circles are respectively located at the four vertices of the square. Two larger identical circles are located at one pair of opposite vertices of the square, and two smaller identical circles are located at the other pair of opposite vertices. In the figure the two large circles are tangent to each other, and each large circle is tangent to the two adjacent small circles. Reasoning: Let the radius of the large circle be R, and the side length of the square be s. The radius of the small circle is 1 cm. Since a large circle is tangent to an adjacent small circle, the distance between their centers is equal to the sum of the two radii, so the side length of the square s = R + 1. The centers of the two large circles are located at opposite vertices of the square, therefore the distance between their centers is the diagonal of the square s√2. Also because the two large circles are tangent, the distance between their centers is 2R. Therefore there is √2(R + 1) = 2R. Solving gives √2R + √2 = 2R, so √2 = (2 - √2)R, R = √2/(2 - √2) = 1 + √2.

method.method_draft: Label the square’s corners as the circle centres, with the large circles at opposite corners and the small circles at the other opposite corners as shown. Let the large radius be R and the square side length be s. From the text, the small radius is 1. Since each large circle touches the adjacent small circles, the distance between adjacent large-small centres is R+1, so s=R+1. The two large circles touch and their centres are opposite corners of the square, so their centre distance is the square diagonal s√2 and also equals 2R. Solve √2(R+1)=2R to get R=1+√2.

method.method_draft: View the line joining the centres of the two large circles as a diagonal of the square. Let the large radius be R. Because the large circles touch, this diagonal has length 2R. In a square, a diagonal makes a 45° angle with each side, so the projection of this diagonal onto a side is 2R cos 45°=R√2.
